title: Where Do You Stand With Your Leader
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note lays out a four-level hierarchy describing how much trust a leader extends to a given team member, ranging from needing explicit instructions to simply being kept informed after the fact. It argues that most leaders don't apply one standard to everyone -- the level reflects a specific team member's track record with that specific leader. The piece is candid that leaders rarely proactively promote someone to the next trust level; instead, team members have to earn it by acting at the higher level and observing how the leader reacts. It ends with a direct challenge to readers to self-assess where they sit and to test moving up a level rather than waiting for permission.
points: Trust with a leader operates on four levels, from asking what to do to simply reporting what was already done.
Leaders typically calibrate trust level per team member based on track record, not a uniform policy.
Leaders rarely proactively promote team members to a higher trust level -- team members must claim it.
Testing a higher trust level by acting and observing the reaction is the recommended path forward.
Trust is described as both earned and negotiated, not simply granted over time.
quotes: Here are the questions and requests team members utilize with leaders ranked in a hierarchy of trust from low to high
It is not unusual for those with little experience, either with an assignment or the leader, to be required to operate at levels 1 or 2.
Leaders generally don’t let team members graduate from one level to the next.
If the trust level is lower than you want it to be, don’t ask for permission to move up the ladder.
Just engage at the next level and see how your leader responds. Take the chance. Trust is not only earned, it is also negotiated.
